title: Keeping his chops with almost no practice
summary: He often takes jobs without having touched the horn in weeks, relying on a natural embouchure while knowing it may eventually fail.

story.theme_name: The reed and horn player's craft: clarinet, sax, tone
story.community_name: Lips, teeth and breath: the physical craft of brass playing

blocks.x: Now that you're not as active playing as you used to be, how do you keep your chops in shape?

That's a -- that all -- that scares me sometimes, because I've been asked that so many times. At my age, and as much as I have played, and everything, I'm supposed to have iron chops. Where's the wood? (Knocks.) (Laughter.)

Sometimes, or many times I've gone on jobs, and guys told me, Herman, can you come down? I say well, I say well, I don't know, but I need the money so damn bad I said well, okay, I'll try it. I go on the job, and we start playing, and I say to the guy, I say you know, I haven't played my horn in such and such and such. He says ah, you're kidding! I say I haven't even taken it out of the case, until tonight. (Laughter.)

Took it out, run some water through it, andyou know, oiled it up, and I've done it so many times. They say oh, say come on down. I say man, I've got no chops. Oh, you know -- you don't need no chops. Come on. Say aw,

man! I say I'm not going to rely on that all the time. I said one of these days it's going to catch me, and I know it. But so far -- so far I've been kind of lucky. I've been -- (Laughs.) But I don't hang out, and deliberately, you know, and wait on that, but when I get around to what's happening, I'll start practicing a lot, when I rest then I'll pick up my horn, and fool around with it for a couple of days, two or three days, and --
